items.text:
Disclosure up front: I work on the manufacturing/OEM side of OTC hearing aids. No product talk below and no links, this is just the part I actually know, and I keep seeing it come up here.

In the last few days this sub has had someone whose aids grab every bit of audio on their phone, two people trying to get aids working with a work computer, and someone who needs iPhone, Mac and PC at once. Different brands, different symptoms, same root cause: "Bluetooth" on a hearing aid spec sheet isn't one thing. There are four, they behave differently, and the sheet almost never tells you which one you're buying.

Bluetooth Classic, the same profile a wireless headset uses. Works with almost any phone regardless of OS version, and it's the only one that reliably shows up on a Windows PC as an audio device. It's also the most power-hungry, so streaming runtime is shortest.

MFi (Made for iPhone), Apple's own low-energy protocol. Works on iPhone, iPad and Mac. There is no MFi on Windows at all, so if you need a work PC, MFi alone will never get you there no matter how good it is on your phone.

ASHA, Google's low-energy streaming for Android. This is the one that catches people out. It isn't simply "Android 10 and up": it also needs a compatible Bluetooth chipset, so support varies by phone model rather than by Android version. Pixels and flagship Samsungs generally work; plenty of budget and mid-range phones don't, even on a current Android build. That's why two people with "the same Android version" get opposite results.

LE Audio with the Hearing Access Profile, the new standard, LC3 codec, and what Auracast is built on. Better sound at lower power, which is the first time those two have moved in the same direction. The catch is the other end: your phone or laptop needs an LE Audio-capable Bluetooth 5.3 radio, and on Windows that support is still patchy, especially on managed work machines.

Two things worth knowing that aren't faults, even though they feel like it.

Your aids taking over all audio on Android is by design. Under ASHA and LE Audio, Android registers hearing aids as an accessibility device and gives them priority for media routing. They reconnect aggressively and pull audio back from speakers on purpose. Nothing is broken; it's the OS doing what it was told.

Android 16 and 17 reworked the audio routing stack. A fair number of recent "it broke after an update" reports are phone-side, not device-side. Your aids didn't change.

One last thing that's purely commercial: when you're comparing battery life between models, ask whether the quoted runtime is standalone or streaming. Those are very different numbers and vendors usually quote the flattering one without saying which it is.

If you're shopping and connectivity matters, the useful questions are: which protocols does it support, which chipset provides them, is there a fallback if my phone doesn't do LE Audio, and what's the streaming runtime.

Happy to be corrected on any brand-specific detail, the fitting-side people here know plenty I don't.

I wasn't sure about your initial post, but if you're a human, you've learned to write like an LLM.
I both love it and hate it... there's times I just want my music to come out my BT speaker. But if I walk away, when I come back my HAs grab the audio.
do you know how Phonak still has Bluetooth Classic on the Sphere, but claims that they will release a software only upgrade to Auracast?

items.text:
Standard bit first. I make OTC hearing aids in China for other brands. Nothing named here, no links.

Someone here rides a motorcycle and said that when a nav prompt comes through, the wind comes with it, louder. That one stuck with me, because it's fixable and hardly anyone knows it is.

Your aids don't mute the room when audio starts. They mix. The stream sits on top of whatever the mics are picking up, at a ratio somebody chose before you ever put them on. Earbuds get away with plugging your ear canal. An open or vented aid can't, and mostly isn't trying to, since the whole design bet is that you still want to hear the doorbell.

Most days that bet is fine. At 60 mph it isn't, and turning the nav volume up doesn't help, you just get two loud things instead of one.

Everyone calls the setting something different. Streaming mix, media balance, mic attenuation, whatever. So don't go asking for a name. Ask for the behavior: while I'm streaming, how far down are the mics, and can you take them further down? Some apps put it on a slider you can move yourself. Others keep it in the fitting software where you'll never see it. If you're OTC with no fitter, you get whatever the app gives you, which is often nothing. That's my side of the industry, not going to dress it up.

Then somebody else told me the opposite and I hadn't thought about it. He's blind as well as deaf. Losing the room the second a stream starts is worse for him than any of this is for me. Same dial, other direction. I don't have a clean answer to that one.

So, careful with it if you're out in traffic. Ambient down means sirens down too. And whoever's yelling at you. If you want it, ask for it as a program you switch into on purpose rather than a change to how streaming always behaves, and keep some ambient in there. Down isn't off.

One bit that isn't a settings problem at all. Air hitting a mic port at speed under a helmet is turbulence right at the port, and gain shaping doesn't undo that. So if pulling the ambient down helps some but not enough, that's probably what's left, and it's a foam and placement problem from there. Though I don't actually know what works under a full face, I've only heard secondhand.

If you want, drop your aids and your phone in a comment and I'll tell you what streaming mix control you're likely to have and where it lives. Model names, that's all I need. I'll get through as many as I can.

items.text:
Same guy who wrote the Bluetooth post a few days back. My factory builds OTC aids in China for other brands, so the thing in your ear may have crossed my bench wearing somebody else's logo. Still not selling anything, still can't name customers.

Two commenters on that post said versions of the same thing and it's been stuck in my head since. Roughly: everyone's got something in their ears now, the stigma's mostly gone, so who is all this shrinking still for. I can't settle the culture part. What I can do is show the invoice. Inside a factory nobody talks about size as a look, it's a spec budget, and every millimeter goes to whoever fought hardest for it in the design review.

What one step up in shell volume actually buys:

Battery is the biggest line item. Going from a cell around 25mAh to the 50mAh class is roughly the difference between streaming most of a workday and dying at lunch. Streaming is the hungry part.

Mic spacing. Directional hearing in a loud restaurant comes from two mics comparing tiny timing differences, and wider spacing gives that math more to work with. Squeeze the mics together and the beamforming goes mushy right where speech lives. A lot of restaurant complaints are geometry problems that get blamed on software.

Antenna. 2.4GHz hates being next to a head, which to a radio is a warm bag of salt water. In a cramped shell the antenna gets folded into whatever corner is left over. When I read dropout complaints here I usually suspect clearance before firmware.

Receiver. Bigger receiver, more real low end, less distortion when you push the volume. Small shells force small receivers, then EQ tries to fake it. Sort of works until it doesn't, and there's a whole separate post in that I keep not writing.

Repairability, which nobody asks about. Dense tiny builds are mostly glued, not screwed. Once the warranty's done, repair quietly turns into replace.

So why doesn't somebody just build the honest big one. Molds cost serious money and every line we run is tooled for small. Retail buyers order off catalogs, and the hero shot is always an aid disappearing behind an ear. Nobody's really lying about any of it, the molds are paid off and the photos work and changing course isn't in anyone's job description, at my place or anywhere else I deal with.

And some of you do still need invisible, I'm not calling that a fake need. There are workplaces where a visible aid still costs you interviews or clients, and earbuds being cool didn't fix that. It's real. It just got to set the defaults for everybody else too.

Same deal as last time. Drop your model and the one thing you'd trade size for. Battery, restaurants, fewer dropouts, whatever it is. I'll go through them and tell you what I know.

items.text:
Same guy from the Bluetooth and shell-size posts. I build OTC aids in China for other brands, so this is the tier I actually know. And yes, I use AI to help me write in English. The knowledge is mine.

This sub argues about OTC constantly and most of the argument is about price. From where I sit the price is the least interesting difference. Here is what actually changes on the line.

Fitting range is the real divide. OTC is built and regulated for mild to moderate loss. That is not marketing caution, it is a hardware decision made early: receiver size, available gain, and how hard the feedback canceller has to work. Push an OTC device at a severe loss and it either can't reach the target or it squeals trying. If your loss is past moderate, no amount of app tweaking fixes that, and anyone selling you otherwise is selling you something.

Self fit versus professional fit is the second one, and it is not just who turns the knob. A prescription fit starts from your audiogram and gets verified in the ear with a probe mic, so the target is measured, not assumed. OTC self fit uses an in app hearing check, which is a decent estimate on good hardware in a quiet room, and a rough one otherwise. Both land in a range. One range is much wider.

Then the parts. Same receiver suppliers, often the same chip families, so the raw components are less different than people assume. Where the money actually goes on a prescription device is the fitting software ecosystem, the clinical validation, the channel margin, and the service that comes with it. Some of that you are paying for and receiving. Some of it you are paying for and never using.

And the honest one about my own side of the industry. OTC quality varies enormously, more than any spec sheet shows, because the barrier to putting a shell around someone else's chip is low. Ask whether the fitting range covers your loss, whether there is a real in ear check rather than four presets, and what the return window is. Forty five days or more, because the first two weeks lie.

One more thing, because it comes up in this sub constantly. A lot of you were told things by a fitter that later turned out not to be true. That every aid pairs with everything. That a bigger device would be wrong for you. That a setting simply isn't available to you. I'm not going to defend that, and I'm not going to tell you it was your fault for not asking better questions.

What you can do is make the claim checkable. Ask which specific protocol the device uses for your phone. Ask to see the fitting range printed on the spec sheet, not described from memory. Ask what the return window is, in writing. A claim that can be checked is a claim that gets made more carefully, and it costs the honest fitter nothing to answer.

If you are on an OTC device right now, drop the model and the one thing about it that annoys you most. I will tell you whether that is a fitting range problem, which no setting will fix, or a settings problem, which you can fix this afternoon. And if it sounds like your loss has moved past what OTC can reach, I will say that too.
